feedback.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)^{2}+y(t)^{2}+x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x \\ 2x+3y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2x+1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)=2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+3y)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+1 & 2y \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get 

$$
{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(0)+1 & 2(0) \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalue of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=1,\text{ }3.$

Finally, since we both have two real and positive eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{source}.$
